questions.q: Draw the structure of 2-bromo-2-methylbutane and state whether it is a primary, secondary, or tertiary haloalkane. Justify your answer by identifying the substitution of the carbon bearing bromine.
questions.a: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane has the structure CH₃–C(Br)(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃. The carbon bearing bromine is bonded to three other carbon atoms (one CH₃, one CH₃, and one CH₂CH₃), making it a tertiary (3°) carbon; hence the compound is a tertiary haloalkane. A wrong answer (e.g., calling it secondary) reveals the student is counting total carbons in the chain instead of counting carbons directly attached to the C–Br carbon.

questions.q: Explain why CH₂=CH–Cl (chloroethene) is classified as a vinylic halide and not a primary haloalkane, even though the halogen-bearing carbon appears to be attached to only one other carbon.
questions.a: In chloroethene, the carbon bearing chlorine is sp²-hybridised (part of a C=C double bond), so the C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character and the compound falls under "compounds containing sp² C–X bond" (vinylic halide), not under alkyl halides which require sp³-hybridised carbon. A student who calls it primary haloalkane is ignoring hybridisation and applying only the carbon-counting rule, which is valid only for sp³ systems.

questions.q: Given the molecular formula C₅H₁₁Br, draw all structural isomers that are primary bromides. Name each using IUPAC nomenclature.
questions.a:
Primary bromides (C–Br on a 1° carbon) for C₅H₁₁Br:
1. CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂Br → 1-bromopentane
2. (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂Br → 1-bromo-3-methylbutane
3. CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂Br → 1-bromo-2-methylbutane
4. (CH₃)₃CCH₂Br → 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane
A missing isomer or incorrect name indicates the student cannot systematically generate carbon skeletons or misidentifies the carbon bearing Br as primary when it is actually secondary (e.g., drawing CH₃CH₂CH₂CHBrCH₃).

questions.q: Compare the C–Br bond in (CH₃)₃CBr (tert-butyl bromide) and C₆H₅CH₂Br (benzyl bromide). Both are on sp³ carbons, yet their reactivity in SN1 reactions differs. Analyse the structural reason.
questions.a: Both have sp³ C–Br bonds, but tert-butyl bromide forms a tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺ stabilised by three electron-donating methyl groups (+I effect), while benzyl bromide forms a benzylic carbocation C₆H₅CH₂⁺ stabilised by resonance delocalisation of the positive charge into the aromatic ring. Resonance stabilisation is stronger than inductive stabilisation, so benzyl bromide undergoes SN1 faster despite being primary. A student who says "both are equally reactive" or "tert-butyl is faster because it's tertiary" misses the resonance stabilisation unique to benzylic systems.

questions.q: A student claims: "All haloalkanes with formula C₄H₉Cl are primary because butane has only primary and secondary carbons." Evaluate this statement and correct it.
questions.a: The statement is false. C₄H₉Cl has four structural isomers: 1-chlorobutane (primary), 2-chlorobutane (secondary), 1-chloro-2-methylpropane (primary), and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane (tertiary). The tertiary isomer exists because the branched skeleton (CH₃)₃C–Cl places chlorine on a carbon bonded to three other carbons. The student incorrectly assumes the carbon skeleton must be linear n-butane; they forgot to consider branched isomers from Class 10 isomerism (c10_chem_cbse_04_005).

questions.q: Design a quick laboratory test to distinguish between 1-bromopropane (primary) and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tertiary) using only aqueous AgNO₃ and ethanol. Predict the observations and explain the underlying principle.
questions.a: Add each halide to warm ethanolic AgNO₃. 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tertiary) reacts rapidly via SN1, forming a cream precipitate of AgBr within minutes because the stable tertiary carbocation forms easily. 1-bromopropane (primary) reacts very slowly or not at all at room temperature because SN1 is unfavourable (unstable primary carbocation) and SN2 is hindered by the weakly nucleophilic ethanol/Ag⁺ medium. A poor answer would suggest both give immediate precipitate or confuse the test with NaI/acetone (Finkelstein), showing misunderstanding of SN1 vs SN2 conditions.
